title: Of the resemblance of children to their fathers
paragraphs: This bundling together of so many varied pieces is done in such a way that I never set pen to paper except when I have too much idle time, and never anywhere but at home; so that it is put together amid endless interruptions and intervals, since occasions sometimes keep me away for months at a stretch. As for the rest, I never correct my first thoughts by any second ones; I may perhaps alter a word here and there, but only to vary the phrasing, not to undo my original meaning. I want to set down the progress of my moods, and let everyone see each piece as it came from the forge. I wish I had begun sooner, so I could have taken better notice of the course of my own changes. A servant of mine, whom I employed to copy out my drafts, thought he had hit on a prize by stealing several pieces from me — the ones he liked best; but it is my consolation that he will be no greater a gainer than I shall be a loser by the theft. I am seven or eight years older since I began, nor has it been without some new acquisition: in that time, by the bounty of age, I have made the acquaintance of the kidney stone. Long converse with the years does not pass off without some such inconvenience. I would have been glad if, out of all the infirmities old age has on offer for long-lived men, it had picked one more welcome to me, for it could not possibly have laid on me a disease I have dreaded so deeply from infancy onward; of all the misfortunes of old age, this is the one I have always feared most. I have often thought to myself that I was going on too long, and that in so long a voyage I was bound to run myself onto some rock or other. I noticed, and have often enough said so, that it was time to depart, and that life should be cut off at the sound and living part — by the surgeon's rule for amputations; and that nature charges very stiff interest from whoever does not pay back the principal at the proper time. And yet I was so far from ready that, in the eighteen months or so I have now been in this uncomfortable condition, I have so accustomed myself to it as to be content to live on with it; and I have found ways to comfort myself, and to hope. So much are men enslaved to their wretched existence that there is no condition so miserable they will not accept it, so long as they may live. Hear Maecenas:
"Debilem facito manu, Debilem pede, coxa, Lubricos quate dentes; Vita dum superest, bene est."
["Cripple my hand, my foot, my hip; shake out my loose teeth: while there is life, it is well." — quoted in Seneca, Ep., 101.]

And Tamerlane, with a foolish kind of humanity, dressed up the bizarre cruelty he practised on lepers — putting to death every one he could find — by claiming he was delivering them from the painful life they led. There was not one of them who would not rather have been a leper three times over than be no longer alive. And when Antisthenes the Stoic, being very sick, cried out, "Who will deliver me from these evils?", Diogenes, who had come to visit him, held out a knife and said, "This will, soon enough, if you wish." — "I do not mean from my life," he replied, "but from my sufferings." Sufferings that only attack the mind I am less sensitive to than most other men, partly out of judgment — for the world treats as terrible, or as worth avoiding at the cost of life, many things that are nearly indifferent to me — and partly through a thick, blunt temperament I have in matters that do not strike me point-blank. That insensibility I regard as one of the best parts of my natural makeup. But essential bodily pains I feel keenly. And yet, having long foreseen them, though with a weak and delicate sight softened by the long and happy health and quiet that God has been pleased to give me most of my time, I had pictured them in my imagination as so unbearable that, in truth, I was more afraid than I have since found I had cause to be. That experience reinforces my belief that most of the faculties of the soul, as we use them, disturb the peace of life more than they actually help it.

I am in a contest with the worst, most sudden, most painful, most deadly, and most incurable of all diseases. I have already had the trial of five or six very long and very painful attacks; and yet either I am flattering myself, or even in this state there is much that can be endured by a man whose soul is free of the fear of death and of the threats, conclusions, and consequences that medicine is forever thundering in our ears. The effect even of pain itself is not so sharp and intolerable as to throw a man of understanding into rage and despair. I have at least this advantage from my stone: that what I could never bring myself to resolve on before — making peace with death and getting acquainted with it — this will finish for me. The more it presses and harasses me, the less afraid I shall be to die. I had already gone so far as to love life only for life's sake; but my pain will dissolve that fondness. And God grant that in the end, should the sharpness of it grow greater than I can bear, it does not throw me into the other no less vicious extreme of desiring and wishing to die!
"Summum nec metuas diem, nec optes:"
["Neither wish for, nor fear, the final day." (Or: "You should neither fear nor desire the last day.") — Martial, x. 7.]
Both are passions to be feared; but one has its remedy much closer at hand than the other.

As for the rest, I have always thought that the rule which so strictly demands a resolute face and a disdainful, indifferent bearing while enduring sickness was a piece of theatre. Why should philosophy, which concerns itself only with life and actions, bother about these external appearances? Let us leave that care to actors and to teachers of rhetoric, who set so much value on our gestures. Let philosophy allow this vocal weakness to disease, if it is not in the heart or in the stomach, and let it permit the ordinary ways of expressing grief — sighing, sobbing, palpitations, going pale — which nature has placed outside our control. Provided the courage stands undaunted, and the tone is not one of despair, let her be satisfied. What does it matter if we wring our hands, so long as we do not wring our thoughts? Philosophy forms us for ourselves, not for others; to be, not to seem. Let her be content with governing our understanding, which she has undertaken to instruct: let her keep the soul, in the fury of a colic, in a condition to know itself, to follow its accustomed path, fighting and enduring pain rather than meanly cringing under it; stirred and heated, yes, but not subdued or conquered in the contest; still able to talk and do other things, up to a point. In such extreme moments, it is cruelty to demand so neat a composure. It is no great matter if we pull a face, so long as the mind plays its part well. If the body finds relief in complaining, let it complain; if thrashing about helps, let it toss and turn at will; if it seems to find the disease easing (as some doctors hold that it eases women in labour) through loud cries, or if shouting merely distracts from the torment, let it roar away. Let us not order this voice to come out, but neither let us stop it. Epicurus not only forgives his wise man for crying out under torment, he actually advises it:
"Pugiles etiam, quum feriunt, in jactandis caestibus ingemiscunt, quia profundenda voce omne corpus intenditur, venitque plaga vehementior."
["Boxers too, when they strike, groan as they do it, because with the force of the voice the whole body is engaged, and the blow lands with greater vehemence." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., ii. 23.]
We have enough on our hands dealing with the disease, without burdening ourselves with these superfluous rules.

I say this in defence of those we commonly see being impatient under the attacks of this malady. As for myself, I have so far carried it off with a slightly better face, contenting myself with groaning rather than crying out — not that I put any great effort into keeping up this outward decorum, for I set little store by such a credit. I allow it as much voice as the pain calls for. But either my pains are not so extreme, or I have more patience than usual. I complain, I admit, and I am a little impatient in a very sharp attack, yet I do not arrive at the degree of despair of the man who:
"Ejulatu, questu, gemitu, fremitibus Resonando, multum flebiles voces refert:"

["Howling, complaining, groaning with a thousand noises, voicing his torment in mournful sounds." (Or: "Wailing, complaining, groaning, mumbling — many lugubrious sounds avail nothing.") — verses by Attius in his Philoctetes, quoted by Cicero, De Finib., ii. 29; Tusc. Quaes., ii. 14.]

I test myself in the depth of my suffering, and have always found that I was able to speak, to think, and to give a rational answer as well as at any other time, though not so steadily, since I am thrown off and interrupted by the pain. When my visitors think I am in the worst of it and so hold back from troubling me, I often test my own strength and start up some conversation, on a subject as far from my present condition as I can contrive. I can do anything by a sudden burst of effort, but I cannot keep it up for long. Oh, what a pity I have not the gift of the dreamer in Cicero, who, dreaming he was sleeping with a girl, discovered he had discharged his stone in the sheets. My pains strangely deaden my appetite that way. In the intervals from this extreme torment, when my ureters are only sore without any great pain, I quickly find myself back in my usual state, since my soul takes no alarm except what is bodily and felt — and that I certainly owe to the care I have taken in preparing myself by meditation against such accidents:
"Laborum, Nulla mihi nova nunc facies inopinave surgit; Omnia praecepi, atque animo mecum ante peregi."
["No new or unexpected face of suffering can arise for me now; I have foreseen them all, and worked through them in my mind beforehand." — Aeneid, vi. 103.]

I am, however, being a little roughly handled for an apprentice, and the change has been sudden and sharp — falling in an instant from a very easy and happy condition of life into the most uneasy and painful that can be imagined. For besides being a disease very much to be feared in itself, it begins with me in a sharper and more severe manner than it usually does with others. My attacks come so thick upon me that I am hardly ever at ease. Yet I have so far kept my mind upright, and provided I can keep on doing so, I find myself in a much better condition of life than a thousand others, who have no other or fewer diseases than what they make for themselves by their failure to meditate.

There is a certain crafty sort of humility that springs from presumption — as, for example, when we confess our ignorance in many things, and are courteous enough to acknowledge that there are in the works of nature some qualities and conditions imperceptible to us, whose causes and methods our understanding cannot discover; by which honest and conscientious admission we hope to win belief that we do understand those things we claim to. We need not go searching for foreign miracles and difficulties; among the things we see every day, it seems to me, there are wonders so incomprehensible that they surpass the difficulty of any miracle. What an astonishing thing it is that the drop of seed from which we are produced should carry in itself the imprint not only of our father's bodily form but even of his thoughts and inclinations! Where in that drop of fluid matter can such an infinite number of forms be contained? And how can they pass on these resemblances by so precarious and irregular a process — that the son shall be like his great-grandfather, the nephew like his uncle? In the family of Lepidus at Rome there were three, not in succession but at intervals, who were born with the same eye covered by a cartilage. At Thebes there was a family that carried from their mother's womb the shape of a spearhead, and any who was not born so was considered illegitimate. And Aristotle says that in a certain nation, where the women were held in common, they assigned the children to their fathers by resemblance.

It is reasonable to believe I inherit this infirmity from my father, for he died terribly tormented by a great stone in his bladder. He was never aware of his disease until the sixty-seventh year of his age, and before that had never felt any warning or symptom of it — not in his kidneys, his sides, or anywhere else — and had lived until then in a happy, vigorous state of health, little prone to infirmity; he then dragged on seven more years with this disease at the painful end of his life. I was born about twenty-five years before the disease seized him, in the time of his most flourishing and healthful condition of body, his third child in order of birth. Where did his propensity to this malady lie hidden all that time? And he being then so far from the infirmity, how could that small part of his substance from which he made me carry off so strong an impression for its share? And how was it so concealed that I did not begin to feel it until forty-five years later? Being, to this hour, the only one out of so many brothers and sisters, all by the same mother, who has ever been troubled with it. Whoever can satisfy me on this point, I will believe him in as many other miracles as he pleases — provided that, as is their way, he does not hand me a doctrine far more tangled and far-fetched than the thing itself, and pass that off as legal tender.

Let the doctors forgive me a little the liberty I take, for by this same infusion and fatal channelling I have inherited a hatred and contempt for their doctrine. My antipathy to their art runs in the family. My father lived seventy-four years, my grandfather sixty-nine, my great-grandfather nearly eighty, without ever tasting any kind of medicine; with them, anything that was not ordinary diet counted as a drug. Medicine is grounded on experience and examples: so is my view. And is this not a clear and very advantageous experiment? I do not think they can find me in all their records three men who were born, raised, and died under the same roof and lived so long under their care. They must necessarily admit here that if reason is not on my side, at least fortune is — and with physicians, fortune goes a great deal further than reason. Let them not now take advantage of me; let them not threaten me in the subdued condition I am in — that would be a low blow. In truth, I have enough the better of them through these family examples that they should be satisfied. Human affairs are not usually so steady; this trial has lasted nearly two hundred years — one hundred and eighty-two, to be exact — for the first of them was born in 1402. It is now, indeed, very reasonable that this experiment should begin to fail us. So let them not reproach me with the infirmities I now suffer; is it not enough that, for my part, I lived forty-seven years in good health? Even if it should be the end of my course, it has been a long run.

My ancestors had an aversion to medicine by some obscure and natural instinct; the very sight of drugs was loathsome to my father. The Seigneur de Gaviac, my uncle on the father's side, a churchman, sickly from birth and yet who stretched that frail life out to sixty-seven years, having once fallen into a furious fever, was told plainly by the doctors that if he would not make use of help (for so they call what is very often a hindrance), he was certain to die. The good man, though horrified at the dreadful verdict, replied: "Then I am a dead man." But God soon made the prediction false. The youngest of the brothers — there were four of them — and by many years the youngest, the Sieur de Bussaguet, was the only one of the family who made use of medicine, on account, I suppose, of his dealings with the other professions, for he was a councillor in the court of Parliament. It went so badly with him that, though to outward appearance he was the strongest in constitution, he died long before any of the rest, save the Sieur de Saint Michel.

It is possible I have inherited this natural antipathy to medicine from them; but even had there been no other consideration in the case, I would have tried to overcome it, since all such conditions as arise in us without reason are vicious — a kind of disease we ought to wrestle with. I may have had this leaning naturally; but I have supported and fortified it by arguments and reasons which have settled the opinion I hold. For I also dislike the way medicine is refused merely for its nasty taste.

I am hardly of that disposition that holds health to be worth buying at the price of all the most painful cauteries and incisions that can be applied. With Epicurus, I think that pleasures should be avoided if greater pains follow, and pains sought if they end in greater pleasures. Health is a precious thing, and in truth the only one that deserves a man to lay out — not only his time, sweat, labour, and goods, but his very life — to obtain it; for without it life is a burden and an injury to us. Pleasure, wisdom, learning, and virtue, without it, wither and vanish. To the most laboured and solid arguments philosophy might urge to the contrary, we need only oppose the image of Plato struck with an epileptic seizure or a stroke; and on that picture defy him to summon the rich faculties of his soul to his help. All means that lead to health can neither be too painful nor too costly for me. But I have some other suspicions that make me strangely doubtful of this whole business. I do not deny there may be some art in it, or that among so many works of Nature there are not things proper for keeping us in health — that is certain. I know very well there are some simple herbs that moisten and others that dry; I know by experience that radishes are windy and senna-leaves purging; and many other such facts I have observed — that mutton nourishes me, and wine warms me; and Solon said that eating was medicine against the disease of hunger. I do not disapprove of the use we make of what the earth produces, nor do I doubt for a moment the power and fertility of Nature, and the way it answers our needs. I see plainly that pikes and swallows live by her laws. But I distrust the inventions of our own minds, our knowledge and craft, for whose sake we have abandoned Nature and her rules, and in which we keep no bounds or moderation. Just as we call the heaping up of the first laws that come to hand justice, and their practice and dispensation are often foolish and very unjust; and as those who scoff at and accuse it do not, even so, blame that noble virtue itself but only the abuse and profanation of that sacred title — so in medicine I greatly honour that glorious name, its propositions, its promises, which would be so useful to mankind; but the prescriptions it foists on us, between you and me, I neither honour nor esteem.

In the first place, experience makes me dread it; for among all my acquaintance, I see no people fall sick so quickly, and stay sick so long, as those who take a lot of medicine; their very health is altered and corrupted by their constant prescriptions. Physicians are not content to deal only with the sick — they will also tamper with health itself, so men should not at any time escape their authority. Do they not, from a long stretch of perfect health, draw the inference of some great sickness about to come? I have been sick often enough, and have always found my illnesses easy enough to bear (and I have tried almost every kind), and as short-lived as anyone's, without their help, without swallowing their foul-tasting doses. The health I have is full and free, with no rule or discipline other than my own habit and pleasure. Any place suits me well enough to stay in, for when I am sick I need no comforts other than what I have when I am well. I am never troubled that I have no doctor, no apothecary, no other professional help — which I see most sick men more distressed by than by their illness. What — do the doctors themselves show us greater happiness and longer lives, that might give us some visible evidence of their skill?

There is not a nation in the world that has not gone many ages without medicine; and those were the first ages — meaning the best and happiest; and a tenth of the world still knows nothing of it; many nations are ignorant of it to this day, where men live more healthfully and longer than we do here, and even among us the common people manage well enough without it. The Romans went six hundred years before they took it on; and after trying it, they banished it from the city at the urging of Cato the Censor, who showed how easy it was to live without it, having himself lived to eighty-five and kept his wife alive to extreme old age — not without medicine, but without a physician, for everything we find healthful to life may be called medicine. He kept his family in health, as Plutarch reports if I am not mistaken, with hare's milk; as Pliny says the Arcadians cured all kinds of disease with the milk of a cow; and Herodotus says the Libyans generally enjoy excellent health by a custom they have of burning and cauterising the veins of the head and temples once their children reach the age of four, by which means they cut off all rheum from running for the rest of their lives. And the country people in our region use nothing, in all kinds of illness, but the strongest wine they can get, mixed with a good deal of saffron and spice, and always with the same success.

To tell the truth, of all this diversity and confusion of prescriptions, what other end or effect is there in the end but to purge the bowels? — which a thousand ordinary herbs will do just as well. And I do not know whether such evacuations are as much to our advantage as they claim, or whether nature does not require a certain quantity of waste to remain, as wine requires its lees to keep it alive. You often see healthy men fall into vomiting and diarrhoea by some accident, and make a great evacuation of waste, without any prior need and without any subsequent benefit — indeed, with damage to their constitution. From the great Plato I lately learned that of the three sorts of motions natural to us, purging is the worst, and no man should take anything to that purpose, unless he be a fool, except in the most extreme necessity. Men disturb and irritate the disease by such contrary attacks. It is the way of living that must gently dissolve and bring it to its end. The violent grappling between drug and disease is always to our loss, since the battle is fought inside us, and the drug is an ally not to be trusted, being in its own nature an enemy to our health, and able to enter our condition only through trouble. Let it alone a little; the general order of things, which takes care of fleas and moles, also takes care of men — if they will have the same patience that fleas and moles have, and leave matters to themselves. We cry out "Bihore!" in vain — it is a way to make us hoarse, not to hurry the business along. It is a proud and unfeeling order: our fears and our despair displease and slow it, instead of inviting it to our relief; it owes its course to the disease as much as to health, and will not let itself be perverted in favour of the one to the prejudice of the other's right, for it would then fall into disorder. Let us, in God's name, follow it; it leads those who follow, and those who will not follow, it drags along — their fury and their physic together. Order a purge for your brain — it will do far better employed there than on your stomach.

When someone asked a Spartan what had made him live so long, he answered: "Ignorance of medicine." And the Emperor Hadrian kept exclaiming as he was dying that the crowd of physicians had killed him. A bad wrestler turned doctor: "Courage," said Diogenes to him, "you have done well — now you will throw those who used to throw you." But they have this advantage, as Nicocles put it, that the sun lights up their successes and the earth covers their failures. Besides, they have a very convenient way of making use of any kind of outcome: for whatever good and healthful effect fortune, nature, or any other cause (and the number is infinite) produces in us, it is medicine's privilege to claim for itself. All the happy events that happen to a patient must, they say, derive from there. The recoveries that have cured me, and a thousand others who do not employ physicians, doctors appropriate to themselves. And as for bad outcomes, they either flatly disown them, putting the blame on the patient on grounds so flimsy they are never short of them — "He lay with his arms out from under the bed-covers," or "He was disturbed by the rattling of a passing coach":
"Rhedarum transitus arcto Vicorum inflexu:"
["The passage of wheels in the narrow turning of the street." — Juvenal, iii. 236.]

or "Someone left the casement open," or "He lay on his left side," or "He had some unpleasant thoughts in his head" — in short, a word, a dream, or a glance seems to them enough excuse to cover their errors. Or, if they prefer, they even make use of our getting worse, and pull off their trick by this means, which can never fail them: by whispering in our ear, when the disease is more inflamed by their drugs, that it would have been much worse had it not been for those remedies. The patient whom they have driven from an ordinary cold into a double quartan fever would have been in a continuous fever without them. They do not much care what harm they do, since it turns to their own profit. In truth, they have reason to demand from their patients a very generous credit; and it had better be an easy one, to swallow things so hard to believe. Plato said it well: doctors are the only men allowed to lie at will, since our health hangs on the vanity and falsity of their promises.

Aesop, an excellent author, whose every grace few men discover, neatly shows us the tyrannical authority physicians wield over poor creatures weakened and subdued by sickness and fear: a sick man, being asked by his doctor what effect the potion he had given him had produced, said, "I have sweated very much." "That's good," said the doctor. Another time, asked how he felt after his medicine: "I have been very cold, and have had a great shivering on me," he said. "That is good," replied the doctor. After the third potion, the doctor asked again how he was: "Why, I find myself swollen and puffed up," he said, "as if I had dropsy." — "That is very well," said the doctor. One of his servants coming in soon after to ask how he felt: "Truly, my friend," he said, "with being too well, I am about to die."

There was a more reasonable law in Egypt, by which the doctor, for the first three days, was to take charge of his patient at the patient's own risk and expense; but after those three days were over, at his own. For what reason should their patron, Aesculapius, have been struck by thunder for restoring Hippolytus from death to life:
"Nam Pater omnipotens, aliquem indignatus ab umbris Mortalem infernis ad lumina surgere vitae, Ipse repertorem medicinae talis, et artis Fulmine Phoebigenam Stygias detrusit ad undas;"

["Then the Almighty Father, angered that any mortal should rise to the light of life from the infernal shades, struck the son of Phoebus with his forked lightning down to the Stygian lake." — Aeneid, vii. 770.]

and his followers be pardoned, who send so many souls from life to death? A doctor, boasting to Nicocles that his art carried great authority: "So it does indeed," said Nicocles, "since it can kill so many people with impunity."

As for the rest, had I been on their council, I would have made my discipline more sacred and more mysterious. They began well, but they have not kept it up. It was a good beginning to make gods and demons the authors of their science, and to use a language all their own in speaking and writing — even though philosophy concludes it folly to try to persuade a man of his own good by an unintelligible route: "Ut si quis medicus imperet, ut sumat:"
"Terrigenam, herbigradam, domiportam, sanguine cassam."
["Describing it by the epithets of an animal trailing with its slime over the herbage, without blood or bones, and carrying its house upon its back — meaning, simply, a snail." — Coste.]

It was a good rule in their art, and one that accompanies all other vain, fantastic, and supernatural arts, that the patient's belief should prepare him with hope and confidence in their effects and operation — a rule they hold to so far as to maintain that the most inexperienced and ignorant doctor is more useful to a patient who has confidence in him than the most learned and experienced one with whom he is not so well acquainted. Even the very choice of most of their drugs has something mysterious and divine about it: the left foot of a tortoise, the urine of a lizard, the dung of an elephant, the liver of a mole, blood drawn from under the right wing of a white pigeon; and for those of us with the stone (so contemptuously do they treat us in our miseries) the excrement of rats pounded into powder, and similar trash and tomfoolery, which has more the face of magical enchantment about it than of any solid science. I leave aside the odd number of their pills, the choice of certain days and feasts of the year, the superstition of gathering their simples at certain hours, and that austere and very wise look and manner which Pliny himself so often mocks. But they have, as I said, failed in this: that they have not added to this fine beginning the making of their meetings and consultations more religious and secret, where no profane person should be admitted, just as the secret ceremonies of Aesculapius were closed. As a result, their irresolution, the weakness of their arguments, predictions, and foundations, the sharpness of their disputes — full of hatred, jealousy, and self-interest — all come to be visible to everyone, and a man must be wonderfully blind not to see that he runs a very great risk in their hands. Who ever saw one doctor approve of another's prescription without taking something away or adding something to it? By which they sufficiently betray their tricks, and make it plain that what they care about is their own reputation, and so their profit, rather than the patient's interest. He was a much wiser member of their tribe who, of old, gave it as a rule that only one doctor should attend a sick person; for if he accomplishes nothing, a single man's failure can bring no great scandal on the art of medicine, while on the contrary the glory will be great if he happens to succeed; whereas when there are many of them, they bring discredit on their calling at every turn, since they do more harm than good. They ought to be content with the perpetual disagreement found in the opinions of the leading masters and ancient authors of this science — which is known only to those well-read — without exposing to the common people the controversies and various judgments which they still feed and prolong among themselves.

Would you like one example of the ancient controversy in medicine? Herophilus locates the original cause of all diseases in the humours; Erasistratus, in the blood of the arteries; Asclepiades, in the invisible atoms of the pores; Alcmaeon, in the excess or defect of our bodily strength; Diocles, in the inequality of the elements that make up the body, and in the quality of the air we breathe; Strato, in the abundance, rawness, and corruption of the food we take; and Hippocrates locates it in the spirits. There is a certain friend of theirs, whom they know better than I, who declares on this subject that "the most important science in our practice, since it is entrusted with our health and preservation, is, by ill fortune, the most uncertain, the most muddled, and shaken by the greatest changes." There is no great harm done in being mistaken about the height of the sun, or about the fraction of some astronomical calculation; but here, where our whole being is at stake, it is not wise to surrender ourselves to the mercy of so many contrary winds.

Before the Peloponnesian War there was no great talk of this science. Hippocrates brought it into repute; whatever he laid down, Chrysippus overturned; after him, Erasistratus, Aristotle's grandson, overturned what Chrysippus had written; after these, the Empirics came forward, who took the opposite line from the ancients in handling this art; when the credit of these began a little to fade, Herophilus set up another sort of practice, which Asclepiades in turn rose up against, and overturned. Then, in their turn, the opinions first of Themison, and then of Musa, and after that those of Vectius Valens, a physician famous through his dealings with Messalina, came into fashion. The empire of medicine in Nero's time was established in Thessalus, who abolished and condemned everything held until his day. His doctrine was refuted by Crinas of Marseilles, who was the first to bring all medical operations under the calendars and motions of the stars, and reduced eating, sleeping, and drinking to hours most pleasing to Mercury and the moon. His authority was soon afterwards displaced by Charinus, a doctor from the same city of Marseilles, who not only challenged all the ancient methods of medicine but also the use of hot baths that had been generally common for so many ages. He made men bathe in cold water, even in winter, and plunged his sick patients in the natural water of streams. No Roman until Pliny's time had ever stooped to practise medicine; that work was done only by Greeks and foreigners, just as today among us French it is done by those who can rattle off some Latin. For, as a very great doctor says, we do not easily accept the medicine we understand, any more than we do the drugs we ourselves gather. If the nations from which we import guaiacum, sarsaparilla, and China wood have physicians, how much value can we imagine they set, by the same recommendation of strangeness, rarity, and high price, on our own cabbage and parsley? — for who would dare to look down on things fetched from so far and obtained at the hazard of so long and dangerous a voyage?

Since these ancient revolutions in medicine, there have been countless others down to our own time, and most of them complete and sweeping changes — like those, for instance, produced by Paracelsus, Fioravanti, and Argentier; for they, as I am told, do not alter only one recipe but the whole framework and rules of the body of medicine, accusing all who practised before them of ignorance and fraud. At this rate, what condition the poor patient must be in, I leave you to judge.

If we were even assured that when they make a mistake their mistake would do us no harm, even if it did us no good, it would be a reasonable bargain to risk making ourselves better with no danger of being made worse. Aesop tells a story that someone who had bought a Moorish slave, believing his black complexion had come about by accident and the ill-treatment of his former master, had him put on a careful course of baths and potions; but the Moor was in no way improved in his tawny colour, and lost his former health entirely. How often do we see doctors blaming each other for the death of their patients? I remember that some years ago there was an epidemic disease, very dangerous and for the most part fatal, that raged in the towns around us. The storm being over which had carried off countless men, one of the most famous doctors of the whole country published a book on the subject soon afterwards, in which, on second thoughts, he admits that bleeding in that disease was the chief cause of so many disasters. Moreover, their own authorities hold that there is no medicine that has not something harmful in it. And if even those that work best in some degree harm us, what must those do that are entirely misapplied? For my own part, even if there were nothing else in the case, I am of the opinion that for those who dislike the taste of medicine, it must be a dangerous and damaging effort to force it down at so unsuitable a time and with so much aversion, and I believe that it troubles a sick person grievously at a moment when he has so much need of rest. And besides, if we consider the grounds on which they usually base the cause of our diseases, they are so slight and delicate that I conclude from this that a very small error in dispensing their drugs may do a great deal of mischief. Now, if a doctor's mistake is so dangerous, we are in a very poor case, for it is almost impossible that he should not often make such mistakes. He must keep too many parts, considerations, and circumstances straight to take his proper aim: he must know the patient's complexion, his temperament, his humours, his inclinations, his actions, even his very thoughts and imaginings; he must be sure of the external circumstances, the nature of the place, the quality of the air and the season, the position of the planets and their influences; he must know, of the disease, the causes, prognoses, symptoms, and critical days; of the drugs, the weight, the power, the country, the form, the age, and the dosing; and he must know how to proportion and mix them properly together, to produce a just and perfect symmetry; and if in all this there is the slightest error, if among so many springs even one is out of order, it is enough to destroy us. God knows how difficult most of these things are to understand: how, for example, shall the doctor find out the true sign of the disease, when every disease is capable of being indicated in countless ways? How many doubts and controversies do they have among themselves about the interpretation of urines? Otherwise, what could account for the continual debates we see among them over diagnosis? How could we excuse the error they so often fall into, of mistaking a fox for a marten? In the illnesses I have had, no matter how little difficulty there was in the case, I never found three of them in one mind: which I mention because I like to bring in examples in which I am myself concerned.

A gentleman in Paris was lately cut for the stone by order of the doctors, and when he was so cut there was no more stone found in his bladder than in the palm of his hand. And in the same place, a bishop who was a particular friend of mine, urgently pressed by the majority of the doctors he consulted to let himself be cut — to which I also, taking their word for it, used my influence to persuade him — was found, when he died and was opened up, to have no malady but in his kidneys. They are least excusable for any error in this disease, because it is in some sense palpable; and that is why I conclude that surgery is much more reliable, since it sees and feels what it does and so works less by guesswork; whereas the physicians have no speculum matricis with which to inspect our brains, lungs, and liver.

Even the very promises of medicine are unbelievable in themselves; for, having to act against various and contrary symptoms that often afflict us at the same time, and that have an almost necessary relation — like the heat of the liver and the coldness of the stomach — they would have us believe that of their ingredients one will heat the stomach and the other will cool the liver; that one is commissioned to go straight to the kidneys, even to the bladder, without spreading its operations on the way, and is to keep its power and virtue through all those turnings and bends right to the place it is designed to serve, by its own occult property; that this one will dry the brain, that one will moisten the lungs. Having mixed up a potion out of all this bundle of things, is it not a kind of madness to imagine or to hope that these different virtues will sort themselves out from one another in this mixture and confusion, and go off to perform so many different errands? I should very much fear that they would either lose or swap their tickets, and disturb one another's quarters. And who can imagine but that in this liquid confusion these powers must spoil, mix up, and ruin one another? And is not the danger still greater when the making up of this medicine is entrusted to the skill and good faith of yet another person, to whose mercy we again hand over our lives?

Just as we have doublet- and breeches-makers, separate trades to clothe us — and we are the better fitted because each of them concerns himself only with his own business and has less to think about than the tailor who does it all — and just as in the matter of food, great persons, for their better convenience and to be better served, have cooks for different jobs, one for soups and broths, another for roasting, instead of which if one cook were to undertake the whole service he could not do it half so well: so also with the cure of our illnesses. The Egyptians had reason to reject this all-purpose trade of physician and to divide the profession: to each disease, to each part of the body, its own particular workman; for that part was more properly and with less confusion looked after, since the man was attending to nothing else. Our doctors are not aware that he who provides for everything provides for nothing; and that the entire government of this microcosm is more than they can take on. While they were afraid of stopping a dysentery for fear they should bring on a fever, they killed a friend of mine who was worth more than the whole lot of them. They balance their own predictions against the present evil; and because they will not cure the brain to the harm of the stomach, they injure both with their quarrelling and disorderly drugs.

As to the variety and weakness of the reasoning in this art, they are more obvious in it than in any other. Aperient medicines are good for a man prone to the stone, since by opening and widening the passages they help carry forward the slimy matter from which gravel and stone are bred, and convey downward what begins to harden and gather in the kidneys. Aperient medicines are dangerous for a man prone to the stone, since by opening and widening the passages they help carry forward the matter that breeds the gravel toward the kidneys, which by their own inclination tend to seize on it; and it cannot but be that a great deal of what has been brought there must stay behind. Moreover, if the medicine happens to meet anything too large to be carried through all the narrow passages it must pass through to be expelled, that blockage, stirred by these aperient drugs and forced into those narrow passages, will stop them and bring about a certain and most painful death. They have the same uniformity in the advice they give us for our regimen. It is good to urinate often, for we know by experience that, letting it lie long in the bladder, we give it time to settle the sediment that will harden into a stone; it is good not to urinate often, for the heavy waste it carries with it will not be voided without force — as we see by experience that a stream running with force washes the ground it crosses much cleaner than the course of a slow, sluggish current. So, it is good to have frequent intercourse with women, for that opens the passages and helps to evacuate gravel; it is also very bad to have frequent intercourse with women, since it heats, tires, and weakens the kidneys. It is good to bathe often in hot water, since that relaxes and softens the places where the gravel and stone lie; it is also bad, for the application of external heat helps the kidneys to bake, harden, and petrify the matter so deposited. For those taking baths, it is most healthful to eat little at night, so that the waters they are to drink the next morning may work better on an empty stomach; on the other hand, it is better to eat little at dinner, so that it does not hinder the operation of the waters while still incomplete, and so as not to overload the stomach so soon after the other labour, but leave the office of digestion to the night, which will do it much better than the day, when the body and soul are constantly in motion. So they juggle and trifle in all their lectures, at our expense; and they could not give me one proposition against which I should not know how to raise an equally strong contrary. Let them, then, no longer rail against those who in the trouble of sickness allow themselves to be gently guided by their own appetite and the advice of nature, and commit themselves to the common fortune.

I have seen on my travels almost all the famous baths of Christendom, and for some years past I have begun to make use of them myself. For I look upon bathing as generally healthy, and I believe we suffer no small inconvenience in our health by having abandoned the custom — generally observed in former times by almost all nations, and still in many — of bathing every day; and I cannot imagine that we are not much the worse for having our limbs crusted and our pores stopped with dirt. As for drinking the waters, fortune has, in the first place, made them not at all unpleasant to my taste; and secondly, they are natural and simple, which at the very least carry no danger with them, even if they do us no good — for which the endless crowd of people of all sorts and complexions who go to them is, I take it, sufficient warranty. And although I have not observed any extraordinary or miraculous effects there — on the contrary, having inquired into it more carefully than usual, I have found all the reports of such operations that get spread around those places to be ill-grounded and false, and those who believe them (as people gladly let themselves be deceived in what they wish) deceived by them — yet I have rarely known anyone who has been made worse by those waters, and a man cannot honestly deny that they sharpen appetite, help digestion, and in some way revive us, provided we do not go too late or in too weak a condition, which I would dissuade anyone from doing. They do not have the power to lift men out of desperate and entrenched diseases, but they can help some light indisposition, or prevent some threatening change. He who does not bring with him cheerfulness enough to enjoy the pleasure of the company he will meet there, and of the walks and exercises to which the loveliness of those places invites us, will doubtless lose the best and most certain part of their effect. For this reason I have so far chosen to go to those most pleasantly situated, where there was the best provision of lodging, food, and company — the baths of Bagnères in France, those of Plombières on the frontiers of Germany and Lorraine, those of Baden in Switzerland, those of Lucca in Tuscany, and especially those of Della Villa, which I have visited most often and at various seasons.

Every nation has its own particular opinions about how to use them, and particular rules and methods for using them; and all of them, as far as I have seen, almost with equal effect. Drinking the waters is not received at all in Germany; the Germans bathe for every disease, and will lie soaking in the water almost from sunrise to sunset. In Italy, where they drink them for nine days, they bathe at least thirty, and commonly drink the water mixed with some other drug to make it work better. Here we are ordered to walk to digest it; there we are kept in bed after taking it until it has worked itself off, with hot cloths constantly applied to our stomachs and feet all the while. And as the Germans have a particular practice of using cupping and scarification in the bath, so the Italians have their doccie — little streams of this hot water brought through pipes — and they bathe with these an hour in the morning and as much in the afternoon for a month at a stretch, on the head, stomach, or whatever other part is afflicted. There are countless other varieties of custom in every country, or rather there is no resemblance at all from one to another. From this you may see that this little branch of medicine to which alone I have submitted, though the one that depends least on art of any, has yet a great share of the confusion and uncertainty so obvious everywhere else in the profession.
The poets put what they have to say with more force and grace; witness these two epigrams:
"Alcon hesterno signum Jovis attigit: ille, Quamvis marmoreus, vim patitur medici. Ecce hodie, jussus transferri ex aede vetusta, Effertur, quamvis sit Deus atque lapis."

["Alcon yesterday touched Jove's statue; though marble, it suffers the force of the doctor: today, ordered to be moved from the old temple where it stood, it is carried out — even though it is a god and a stone." — Ausonius, Ep., 74.]
and the other:
"Lotus nobiscum est, hilaris coenavit; et idem Inventus mane est mortuus Andragoras. Tam subitae mortis causam, Faustine, requiris? In somnis medicum viderat Hermocratem:"

["Andragoras bathed with us, supped cheerfully, and the same was found dead in the morning. Do you ask, Faustinus, the cause of so sudden a death? In his dreams he had seen the doctor Hermocrates." — Martial, vi. 53.]
On which I will tell two stories.

The Baron de Caupène in Chalosse and I share between us the patronage of a great benefice at the foot of our mountains, called Lahontan. With the inhabitants of this corner it is just as is said of those of the Val d'Angrogne: they used to live a peculiar sort of life, their habits, clothes, and manners distinct from other people, ruled and governed by certain particular laws and customs handed down from father to son, to which they submitted with no other constraint than reverence for custom. This little community had continued from the earliest times in such a happy condition that no neighbouring judge had ever been put to the trouble of looking into their affairs; no lawyer was ever retained to give them counsel, no stranger ever called in to settle their differences; nor was any of them ever seen to go begging. They avoided all alliances and trade with the outside world, so as not to corrupt the purity of their own government; until, as the story goes, one of them, within living memory, his mind spurred on by a noble ambition, took it into his head — in order to bring his name into credit and reputation — to make one of his sons something more than ordinary. Having sent him to learn writing in a neighbouring town, he made him at last a fine village notary. This fellow, having acquired such dignity, began to despise their old customs and to chatter into the people's ears about the splendours of the rest of the nation. The first trick he played was to advise a friend, whom someone had offended by sawing off the horns of one of his goats, to make his complaint to the royal judges thereabouts; and so he went on, from one to another, until he had spoiled and confounded the lot. On the heels of this corruption, they say, there came another, and one of worse consequence, by means of a doctor who, having fallen in love with one of their daughters, wanted to marry her and live among them. This man first began to teach them the names of fevers, colds, and abscesses; the seat of the heart, liver, and intestines — a science till then completely unknown to them; and instead of garlic, with which they used to cure every kind of disease, however painful or extreme, he taught them, even for a cough or any little chill, to take strange mixtures, and so began to make a trade not only of their health, but of their lives. They swear that until then they had never noticed the evening air being harmful to the head; that drinking when hot was injurious; or that the autumn winds were unhealthier than those of spring. Since this use of medicine, they find themselves burdened with a legion of unaccustomed diseases, they notice a general decline in their old vigour, and their lives are cut shorter by half. That is the first of my stories.

The other is that before I was afflicted with the stone, hearing that the blood of a he-goat was held in great esteem by many, and looked upon as a celestial manna rained down on these latter ages for the good and preservation of men's lives — and having heard it spoken of by men of understanding as an admirable drug, of infallible effect — I, who have always thought myself liable to all the accidents that can befall other men, had a mind, in my perfect health, to stock myself with this miracle; so I gave orders for a goat to be fed at home according to the recipe. He had to be taken in the hottest month of summer, given only aperient herbs to eat, and white wine to drink. By chance I came home the very day he was to be killed; and someone came and told me the cook had found two or three large balls in his paunch, that rattled against one another among what he had eaten. I was curious to have all his innards brought before me, and when I had the skin that enclosed them cut, out tumbled three big lumps, as light as sponges, so that they seemed to be hollow, but otherwise hard and firm on the outside, spotted and shot through with various dead colours. One was perfectly round and the size of an ordinary ball; the other two slightly smaller, of an irregular roundness, as if they had not yet reached full growth. I gather, on inquiry from people used to opening up these animals, that it is a rare and unusual occurrence. It is likely these are stones of the same nature as ours; and if so, it must be a very idle hope on the part of those who have the stone to find their cure in the blood of a beast that was himself about to die of the same disease. To say that the blood does not share in this contagion, and does not therefore lose its supposed virtue, is hardly credible — it is rather to be thought that nothing is bred in a body except by the cooperation and communication of all its parts: the whole mass works together, though one part contributes more to the work than another, according to the variety of operations; so it is very likely there was some stone-making quality in every part of this goat. It was not so much fear of the future, or concern for myself, that made me curious about this experiment; it is because in my household, as in many other families, the women keep up such little oddments for serving the people, using the same recipe in fifty different diseases — a recipe they will not take themselves, and yet they crow about it when it happens to succeed.

As for the rest, I honour physicians — not according to the precept of necessity (for to that passage another may be opposed, where the prophet rebukes King Asa for having recourse to a doctor), but for themselves, having known many very good men in that profession, and most worthy to be loved. I do not attack them; it is their art I rail against, and I do not blame them much for making their advantage out of our folly — most men do the same. Many callings, both nobler and humbler than theirs, have no other foundation or support than public abuse. When I am sick I send for them, if they are nearby, only to have their company, and I pay them as others do. I let them order me to keep warm, because I naturally like to; and to prescribe leeks or lettuce in my broth, or order me white wine or claret; and so on with everything else that is a matter of indifference to my palate and habit. I know perfectly well that I am doing nothing for them by it, because harshness and strangeness are part of the very essence of medicine. Lycurgus ordered wine for sick Spartans. Why? Because they detested drinking it when they were well — just as a gentleman, a neighbour of mine, takes it as an excellent medicine in his fever, because he naturally has a horror of the taste of it. How many of them do we see in my own line of mind, who scorn taking medicine themselves, live freely at table, and live a life quite contrary to what they prescribe for others? What is this but flatly to take advantage of our simple-mindedness? — for their own lives and health are no less dear to them than ours are to us, and so they would adapt their practice to their own rules, if they did not themselves know how false those rules are.

It is the fear of death and of pain, impatience with disease, and a violent and reckless desire for an immediate cure that so blinds us; it is pure cowardice that makes our belief so pliable and easy to impose on. And yet most men do not so much believe as acquiesce and permit; for I hear them grumbling and complaining as we do; but they settle in the end on "What else can I do?" — as if impatience were of itself a better remedy than patience. Is there one of those who have let themselves be persuaded into this miserable submission who does not equally surrender himself to all sorts of impostures? Who does not put himself at the mercy of anyone shameless enough to promise him a cure? The Babylonians used to carry their sick into the public square; the doctor was the public itself: everyone who passed by, obliged out of humanity and civility to ask after their condition, gave some advice from his own experience. We do little better; there is not so simple a woman whose gossip and home brews we do not make use of. And, in keeping with my temperament, if I had to take medicine I would sooner choose theirs than any other, because at least, if they do no good, they will do no harm. What Homer and Plato said of the Egyptians — that they were all physicians — may be said of every nation: there is not a man among any of them who does not boast of some rare recipe, and who will not try it out on his neighbour if he is allowed. The other day I was in a company where someone or other in my own line brought us word of a new sort of pill made up of more than a hundred ingredients. It made us very merry, and was a singular consolation — for what rock could withstand such a battery? And yet I am told by those who have tried it that the smallest grain of gravel did not deign to stir.
I cannot take my hand off the paper before I have added a word concerning the assurance they give us of the reliability of their drugs, derived from the experiments they have made.

The greater part — I should say more than two-thirds — of the medicinal virtues consist in the quintessence or occult property of simples, of which we can have no other knowledge than use and custom; for quintessence is nothing other than a quality whose cause our reason cannot find out. In such proofs, those they claim to have acquired by the inspiration of some demon I am content to accept (for I do not meddle with miracles); and likewise the proofs drawn from things which, by some other route, often come into use among us — as if in the wool we usually clothe ourselves with, some occult drying property happened to be found out for curing chilblains, or as if in the radish we eat for food some aperient operation were discovered. Galen reports that a man happened to be cured of leprosy by drinking wine out of a vessel into which a viper had crept by chance. In that example we find the means and a very likely guide and conduct to the experience, as we do in those that physicians claim to have been directed to by the example of some beasts. But in most of their other experiments, in which they say they have been led by fortune and have had no other guide than chance, I find the progress of the discovery incredible. Suppose a man looking round him at the infinite number of things — plants, animals, metals; I do not know where he would begin his trial. And even if his first fancy fixed him on an elk's horn — which already takes a fairly pliant and easy belief — he will still find himself just as perplexed in his second operation. There are so many diseases and so many circumstances put before him that, before he can reach the certainty of the point to which the perfection of his experience should rise, human sense will be at the end of its lesson; and before he can, among this infinity of things, work out what this horn is, among so many diseases what epilepsy is, the many complexions in a melancholy person, the many seasons in winter, the many nations in the French, the many ages in age, the many celestial changes in the conjunction of Venus and Saturn, the many parts in man's body — even in a single finger — and being, in all this, guided neither by argument, conjecture, example, nor divine inspiration, but only by the sheer motion of fortune, it would have to be a perfectly artificial, regular, and methodical fortune. And after the cure has been carried out, how can he assure himself it was not because the disease had simply run its course, or the effect of chance, or the operation of something else he had eaten, drunk, or touched that day? Or by virtue of his grandmother's prayers? And, moreover, had this experiment been perfect, how many times was it repeated, and this long string of chances and concurrences strung together anew by chance to settle a sure rule? And when the rule has been settled, by whom, I ask? Out of so many millions, only three men take it upon themselves to record their experiments: must fortune just happen to hit on one of them? What if another, and a hundred others, have done contrary experiments? We might perhaps have some light on this if all the judgments and arguments of men were known to us; but that three witnesses, three doctors, should lord it over all mankind is against reason: human nature would have had to depute and choose them, and they would have had to be declared our overseers by express authority.
"TO MADAME DE DURAS.

"MADAME, — The last time you honoured me with a visit, you found me at work on this chapter, and since these trifles may one day fall into your hands, I also want them to bear witness to how greatly the author will take any favour you may be pleased to show them. You will find in them the same air and manner you have observed in his conversation; and although I could have borrowed some better or more attractive dress than my own, I would not have done so, for I want nothing more from these writings than to be present to your memory just as I naturally am. The same qualities and faculties you have been pleased to frequent and welcome with much more honour and courtesy than they deserve, I would set down (but without alteration or change) in one solid body, that may perhaps last some years, or some days, after I am gone — where you may find them again whenever you wish to refresh your memory of me, without putting yourself to any greater trouble; nor are they worth it. I should like you to continue your friendship to me by the same qualities by which it was acquired.

"I am not at all ambitious that anyone should love and esteem me more dead than living. The humour of Tiberius is ridiculous, but yet common, who was more anxious to extend his fame to posterity than to make himself welcome to the men of his own time. If I were one of those to whom the world might owe praise, I would gladly give up half of it to have the other half in hand: let the praises come quick and crowding around me, more thick than long, more full than lasting — and let them cease, in God's name, with my own awareness of them, when the sweet sound can no longer reach my ears. It would be a foolish whim to try, now that I am about to leave the company of men, to offer myself to them by some new commendation. I make no account of the goods I could not employ in the service of my life. Such as I am, I would rather be so elsewhere than on paper: my craft and industry have always been turned to making myself good for something; my studies, to teach me to do, not to write. I have made it my whole business to shape my life: this has been my trade and my work; I am less a writer of books than anything else. I have wanted understanding for the service of my present and real conveniences, not to lay up a stock for posterity. He who has something of value in him, let him show it in his behaviour, in his ordinary talk, in his courtships and his quarrels: in his play, his bed, his table, the management of his affairs, his household. Those I see making good books in poor breeches ought to have mended their breeches first, if they had taken my advice. Ask a Spartan whether he would rather be a good orator or a good soldier; and if I were asked the same question, I would rather be a good cook, if I did not already have one to serve me. My God! Madame, how I should hate such a recommendation — of being a clever fellow at writing, and an ass and a nullity in everything else! Yet I would rather be a fool both here and there than to have made so poor a choice in employing my talent. And I am so far from expecting to gain any new reputation by these follies, that I shall think I come off well enough if I lose nothing by them of the little I had before. For besides that this dead and mute portrait will subtract from my natural being, it bears no resemblance to my better days, but is much fallen off from my former vigour and cheerfulness, growing faded and withered: I am near the bottom of the barrel, which begins to taste of the lees.

"As for the rest, Madame, I should not have dared to make so bold with the mysteries of medicine, considering the esteem in which you and so many others hold it, had I not been encouraged by their own authors. I think there are of these among the old Latin writers but two, Pliny and Celsus; if these ever fall into your hands, you will find that they speak much more roughly of their art than I do — I but pinch it, they cut its throat. Pliny, among other things, jokes that when they are at the end of their rope, they have a pretty trick to save themselves, by recommending their patients (whom they have teased and tormented with their drugs and diets to no purpose) some to vows and miracles, others to the hot baths. (Don't be angry, Madame; he is not speaking of the ones in our parts, which are under the protection of your house, and all Gramontins.) They have a third way of saving their own credit, of getting us off their hands and shielding themselves from the reproaches we might cast in their teeth about how little we have improved, after they have had us so long in their care and have not one more invention left to amuse us with: which is to send us to the better air of some other country. This, Madame, is enough; I hope you will allow me to return to my discourse, from which I have so far digressed, the better to entertain you."

It was, I think, Pericles, who being asked how he did, said: "You may judge by these," showing some little scrolls of parchment he had tied about his neck and arms. By which he meant that he must be very sick indeed when he had been driven to the point of resorting to such idle and vain fopperies, and of letting himself be rigged out in this fashion. I dare not promise that I may not one day be foolish enough to commit my life and death to the mercy and direction of the doctors. I may fall into such a frenzy; I cannot guarantee my future steadfastness. But then, if anyone asks me how I am, I too may answer, like Pericles, "You may judge by this," showing him my hand clutching six drachms of opium. It will be a very plain sign of a violent sickness: my judgment will be quite out of order; if once fear and impatience get such an advantage over me, it may well be concluded that there is a frightful fever in my mind.

I have taken pains to plead this cause, which I understand only moderately, a little to back up and support the natural aversion to drugs and the practice of medicine I have inherited from my ancestors — so that it may not be a merely stupid and unthinking aversion, but have a little more shape; and also so that those who shall see me so stubborn in my resolution against all the exhortations and threats given me, when my infirmity presses hardest, may not think it is mere obstinacy, or anyone be ill-natured enough to judge it to be from any motive of vanity: for it would be a strange ambition to seek to win honour by an action my gardener or my groom can perform just as well as I. I have not a heart so swollen and windy that I should trade so solid a pleasure as health for an airy and imaginary one: glory, even the glory of the Four Sons of Aymon, is too dearly bought for a man of my disposition if it costs him three pounding fits of the stone. Give me health, in God's name! Those who love medicine may also have good, weighty, and convincing reasons; I do not hate opinions contrary to my own. I am so far from being annoyed to see a discrepancy between my judgments and other men's, and from making myself unfit for the society of men because they hold a different view or party from mine, that on the contrary — variety being the most general way nature has followed, and more so in souls than in bodies, as souls are of a more pliant substance and more susceptible to forms — I find it much rarer to see our moods and designs coincide and agree. And there never were in the world two opinions exactly alike, any more than two hairs, or two grains: their most universal quality is diversity.
